title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, ADRs
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview

This document consolidates cross-cutting architecture and engineering standards that govern how teams design, implement, deploy, and operate Redwood services and model-serving infrastructure. It covers API design and versioning, coding and review standards, infrastructure (IaC) conventions, model-serving-specific constraints (latency, batching, caching), observability expectations, performance SLOs, and the policy and template for ADRs (architecture decision records).

Goals
- Provide a single, actionable reference for engineers and architects.
- Reduce ambiguity that causes integration and operational errors.
- Ensure production reliability and consistent developer ergonomics across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Principles (applies to all sections)
1. Developer-first: APIs and infra should be discoverable, well-documented, and ergonomically consistent across languages.
2. Production-first: Make operational cost, latency, and reliability primary design inputs.
3. Observable-by-default: Services must emit structured telemetry (metrics, traces, logs) and expose dashboards.
4. Secure-by-default: Secrets, keys, and customer data must follow the security-and-compliance playbook.
5. Iterative decisions: Major trade-offs must be captured as ADRs and revisited on significant changes.

1) API Standards
Introduction
APIs are the integration surface for customers and internal services. Follow the conventions below to ensure consistency, ease of use, and safe rollouts.

Naming and Versioning
- Use path-versioning: /v1/, /v2/. No breaking changes permitted under the same major version.
- Resource-oriented endpoints: verbs for actions only when necessary. Prefer /v1/models/{model_id}/infer over /v1/infer-model.

Request / Response practices
- Use JSON for request/response payloads. Field naming: camelCase for public APIs (SDKs are camelCase-first). Internal service-to-service APIs may be snake_case where preferred by platform teams, but document it explicitly.
- Use explicit request envelopes for optional runtime controls: e.g., {"model":"redwood-13b-q4", "timeout_ms": 5000, "trace_id": "..."}.
- Include idempotency tokens on mutating requests: header X-Idempotency-Key.

Errors and Status Codes
- Use standard HTTP status codes. Prefer 4XX for client errors and 5XX for transient server issues.
- Error envelope: {"code":"string","message":"string","details":{}}. Provide a stable error code namespace (examples: model_not_found, quota_exceeded, rate_limit).

Pagination and Large Results
- Use cursor-based pagination for large lists: {"next_cursor":"...", "items": [...]}.
- Avoid offset-based pagination for high-scale endpoints.

Rate Limits and Quotas
- Expose headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.
- Document per-route limits in the API spec and enforce via central gateway.

OpenAPI and SDKs
- All public REST APIs must publish an OpenAPI v3 spec in the openapi/ folder of the repo and be validated in CI.
- SDKs must be generated from the canonical OpenAPI where possible and provide idiomatic wrappers.

Stability and Deprecation
- Deprecation policy: at least 90 days’ notice for non-critical changes, 180 days for breaking removal of public fields. Document timeline and automated linting for deprecated fields in SDKs.

Example endpoint summary
- POST /v1/generate: text generation entrypoint. Body: {prompt, model, maxTokens, temperature}.
- POST /v1/embeddings: compute embeddings. Body: {input, model}.
- GET /v1/models: catalog.

2) Coding Standards
Scope and languages
- Backend services (runtime, orchestration): Go 1.20+ is preferred.
- Client SDKs: TypeScript/Node, Python.
- Research and evals: Python.

Formatting and linting
- Go: gofmt, go vet, staticcheck.
- TypeScript: prettier, eslint with recommended rules.
- Python: black, isort, flake8 where appropriate.
- CI enforces formatting and lints on pull requests.

Testing and Coverage
- Unit tests for business logic; integration tests for external dependencies (S3, Kafka, GPU runtime).
- Target coverage: minimum 70% for libraries, 85% for critical runtime packages. Coverage gates are applied to new or modified code paths; absolute coverage thresholds are discouraged for non-critical repos.
- Contract tests for SDKs against a staging OpenAPI endpoint.

Code Review and Commits
- Require at least one approving reviewer from the owning team and one reviewer from a cross-functional area for infra-impacting changes.
- Commit message format: <scope>(<component>): short description
  - Example: runtime(batch): improve kv cache eviction metrics

Repository Structure and Module Rules
- One service per repository for backend runtime components. Shared libraries live in org-wide "libs/" repositories with stable semver.
- Modules must follow semantic versioning. Breaking changes require an ADR and a major-version bump.

3) Infrastructure Standards (IaC, Networking, Secrets)
IaC
- Terraform is the canonical IaC tool for cloud deployments. Use the shared modules in eng-infra/terraform-modules.
- Keep state in remote backends (S3 + DynamoDB lock for AWS).
- Tagging standard: {owner:TBD, product:redwood, env:prod|staging|dev, cost_center:team_code}.

Networking and Security
- VPC per environment with strict subnet segmentation for control plane, runtime, and customer-dedicated networks.
- All customer-sensitive network access must be confined to Private deployments or Dedicated VLANs.
- Use Security Groups/Network Policies with the least privilege.

Secrets and Keys
- Secrets stored in AWS Secrets Manager or customer-managed KMS/HSM for Private deployments. Never check secrets into git.

Deployments and Rollouts
- Supported strategies: canary (preferred), blue-green for major infra upgrades.
- Canary standard: 5% -> 20% -> 100% with automated checks and a minimum 1 hour observation window between steps for standard services. For model-serving runtime (high-risk), use extended observation (24 hours).

Ownership and Runbooks
- Each component must list an owner and a primary on-call rotation.
- Publish a runbook in the service repo: runbooks/README.md. Include recovery steps for P0/P1, escalation, and SLAs.

4) Model-Serving Standards (runtime-specific)
Design Constraints
- Models must be annotated with: architecture (e.g., transformer-decoder), typical sequence length, quantization profile, GPU memory requirements, and compatible runtime version. This metadata lives in the model catalog.

Batching and KV Cache
- Runtime should expose knobs for dynamic batching windows and max batch size. Default dynamic batching target: 8–16 tokens/req for low-latency workloads; higher batching targets for throughput-oriented endpoints.
- KV cache enablement: cache hit rate target >= 60% for long-session chat workloads when prefix caching is enabled. Monitor cache eviction and fragmentation.

GPU Utilization and Scheduling
- Target average GPU utilization per-device: 60–75% under steady-state. Over 85% sustained indicates capacity constraints and requires scaling or model-variant routing.

Model Variants and Fallbacks
- Model variants must be compatible at the API contract level. If primary model is unavailable, the router may fallback to a compatible variant (e.g., lower-precision quantized model) with documented quality trade-offs.

Quality Regression Controls
- Every model rollout requires an eval suite (prompt-set) with pass/fail gates. Use Redwood Optimize to run automatic regression checks. Gate failures block canary promotion.

5) Observability Standards (metrics, logs, traces, dashboards)
Telemetry primitives
- Metrics: all services must export Prometheus metrics with a common prefix (redwood_).
  - Required metrics: request_total (labels: route, method, model), request_duration_seconds (histogram), error_total (labels: route, error_code), batch_size_distribution, kv_cache_hit_rate.
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry tracing with W3C trace context propagation. Include trace_id in logs for correlation.
- Logs: structured JSON logs (timestamp, level, service, trace_id, span_id, message, extra). Use INFO for successful operations and WARN/ERROR for anomalies.

Dashboards and Alerts
- Per-service dashboards: latency p50/p95/p99, error rate, throughput (rps), CPU/GPU utilization, queue lengths, and batch sizes.
- Alerts: alert on sustained error rate > 0.5% over 5m or latency p99 increase > 50% over baseline for 5m. Adjust thresholds per-service; justify deviations in ADR.

SLOs and Error Budgets
- Default SLOs: availability 99.95% monthly for API control plane endpoints; model inference SLOs depend on product SLAs (see Performance section).
- Each team is responsible for tracking and consuming their SLOs in the stability dashboard and specifying mitigation when error budget burn exceeds 25% per quarter.

6) Performance Standards and Benchmarks
Benchmarks and Labs
- Maintain a canonical benchmarking harness in applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness for latency and cost-per-token experiments.
- Benchmark runs must include single-request p95/p99, throughput (tokens/sec), and cost-per-token estimates for each target hardware profile.

Latency targets (guideline)
- Hosted API (interactive text gen): p50 < 120ms, p95 < 350ms, p99 < 900ms for typical 512-token requests on the curated low-latency models.
- Embeddings: p50 < 50ms, p95 < 150ms.
- Batched throughput endpoints: throughput and batch latency trade-offs must be documented per route.

Load testing and Capacity Planning
- Run planned load tests before major launches using eng-sre capacity-planning playbook.
- Capacity targets: maintain 1.3x headroom for traffic spikes for Hosted environments, tighter for Dedicated (contracted) capacity—follow customer SLA commitments.

Performance regression process
1. Detect via continuous benchmarking and PR perf checks.
2. Triage in regression-triage: reproduce in perf lab and collect traces/profiles.
3. Create an incident/ADR if the change requires architectural work.

7) Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
Purpose
- Capture the rationale behind important architecture or standards changes so future engineers can understand trade-offs.

Template (use this exact header fields)
- ADR ID: incremental numeric identifier (e.g., ADR-2026-042)
- Title: short descriptive title
- Status: proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded
- Date: YYYY-MM-DD
- Authors: list of authors
- Context: background and forces driving the decision
- Decision: what is decided, succinctly
- Consequences: operational, security, cost, and migration implications
- Rollout Plan: steps to implement and validate
- Related ADRs / pages: list of links

Process
- Create a draft ADR in the architecture-and-standards repo under adr/ with a PR.
- At least one reviewer from architecture and one from eng-sre must approve.
- Once accepted, move status to accepted and add a short changelog entry in the monthly architecture newsletter.

Example ADR summary
- ADR ID: ADR-2026-042
- Title: Standardize runtime API surface for streaming responses
- Status: accepted
- Date: 2025-11-03
- Decision: Adopt server-sent events (SSE) for public HTTP streaming endpoints and gRPC stream for internal service-to-service streaming when low-latency metadata exchange is required.
- Consequences: SDKs need to implement SSE polyfills for browsers; gateway must preserve streaming semantics and timeouts.

Governance and Exceptions
- Exceptions to these standards require an ADR that documents the reason and a sunset plan.
- Security or legal constraints (e.g., customer regulatory requirements) may override defaults; document exceptions with the security-and-compliance team.

Operational playbooks and runbooks (where to find them)
- Runbooks live in each service repo under /runbooks. For centralized operational guidance see: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks and /confluence/eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build.

Appendix: Useful snippets
OpenAPI example (minimal)
openapi: 3.0.1
info:
  title: Redwood Inference API
  version: v1
paths:
  /v1/generate:
    post:
      summary: Generate text
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                prompt:
                  type: string
                model:
                  type: string
      responses:
        '200':
          description: successful response

Example alerting rules (Prometheus-style pseudo)
- High error rate: increase(error_total{job="runtime"}, 5m) / increase(request_total{job="runtime"}, 5m) > 0.005
- Latency spike: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route)) > baseline_p99 * 1.5
